title: Microsoft’s Agent 365 tackles multicloud AI governance
summary: For more than 20 years, I have watched cloud computing evolve from a relatively simple extension of enterprise infrastructure into a distributed collection of platforms, services, data stores, applications, and now AI agents. One lesson has remained clear: Enterprises don’t operate in the clean, single-vendor environments that providers portray in their marketing. They operate in heterogeneous environments. They always have. A company that has standardized on one public cloud for core infrastructure might use another for a specialized data platform, rely on Salesforce for customer engagement, run analytics in Databricks or Snowflake, and deploy dozens of software-as-a-service applications throughout the business. Add the current explosion of AI models, agent platforms, developer tools, and local AI clients, and the need for unified management becomes much more urgent. This is what makes Microsoft’s Agent 365 announcement so significant. Microsoft is positioning Agent 365 as a common control plane for managing, governing, securing, and measuring the value of AI agents across both Microsoft and non-Microsoft platforms. It’s more than another cost dashboard; it acknowledges that multicloud is now the standard operating model for most enterprises. It’s also a refreshingly practical position from a company that has historically built some of the industry’s most successful proprietary technology ecosystems. Enterprises are heterogeneous The biggest disconnect in cloud computing has often been between what providers want customers to do and what customers actually need to do. Providers prefer that enterprises consolidate around their platforms. It makes commercial sense. A larger footprint means more consumption, stronger customer retention, and a better opportunity to sell adjacent services. However, enterprise architecture doesn’t work that way. title: Who wants a lamp that wants to be wanted?
summary: In the 2004 comedy Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy , the dim-witted Brick Tamland (played by Steve Carell) blurts, “I love lamp!” In 2004, it was a joke. Now it’s a business plan. A burgeoning industry is working hard to make us all “love lamp.” But how do you make a lamp lovable? The Apple research In February of last year, I told you about an Apple research project , and the paper it produced, aimed at giving a lamp a personality. Created by Apple’s Machine Learning Research division, the ELEGNT project used AI to give a non-humanoid desktop robot the expressiveness of a person or a pet. In other words, Apple built something with the body of a lamp and the body language of a pet. The robot lamp was designed to “pay attention” to the user’s actions and words, and respond like it understood. The lamp could speak, but its signature trick was body language: nodding, shaking, and tilting its “head,” wagging a figurative “tail” with its arm, and leaning forward and “gazing” to simulate interest and attention. Open a book, and the lamp turned to face it, lit the page, and “read” along, adding related information with a projector. The ELEGNT project, which drew on Pixar’s 1986 short Luxo Jr. , helped spark today’s fascination with lamps that have personalities, even though Apple shows no sign of wanting to sell a lovable lamp. Its approach of expressive movement resembles what’s been reported about Apple’s desktop robot, code-named J595. The unannounced, unnamed product is a tabletop robot that can control smart-home devices and has a 9-inch screen mounted on a motorized arm. It’s basically an iPad attached to a robot arm that moves and tilts for both personality and practicality, such as keeping the screen trained on you during a FaceTime call no matter where you move. Apple’s desktop robot is expected to cost about $1,000 and come out in 2027 or 2028. title: OpenAI’s GPT‑6.2 correction means you get less AI for the same fee
summary: OpenAI has corrected a billing error that undercounted usage of its GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models, warning customers that the same workloads will now consume more of their subscription allowances and cause them to reach usage limits up to 40% faster. The correction, disclosed by Thibault Sottiaux, who works on ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI, affects most users of the two models. Astra users will reach their plan limits 40% faster than they did last week, while Sol users will reach their limits 25% faster, Sottiaux said in a post on X . “We made a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users,” Sottiaux wrote. “We’ve fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan’s usage allowance,” he added. OpenAI said other models were not affected and that it would not retrospectively charge customers for the difference in past usage. As compensation, Sottiaux said, the company will give “one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business.” Nine days of discounted compute OpenAI released the two models in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. In its launch announcement , it said Astra set new benchmark highs “at less than a third of the cost per task of GPT‑6 Astra.” Sottiaux’s post did not say what caused the discount, which users escaped it, or what the corrected metering rates are. Nor did it say whether “40% faster” means usage is consumed 1.4 times as fast or that the allowance now lasts 40% less time. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, credited OpenAI for disclosing the error and not billing for past usage. But he said the episode exposes a budgeting gap. “OpenAI did not raise the price of GPT-6.2. It changed how much work the price buys, and that is the harder number to budget,” Gogia said. title: Where Does One Sanskrit Word End and the Next Begin?
summary: What can a grammar contribute to a neural network reading Sanskrit? In TransLIST, the Sanskrit Heritage analyser uses a lexicon and explicit rules to propose words that could underlie a written passage. The network receives these candidates alongside the characters and predicts where the words divide and which sounds to restore. In one test, access to the analyser improved the recovery of complete sentences. The size of the gain depended on whether the comparison model had only characters or also had short character sequences. For a scholar, a different question follows. Does seeing the alternatives help a reader correct a plausible mistake? Does seeing the grammatical reason for each alternative help further? Evidence from annotation studies suggests that readers can save time. Measuring whether they choose a better reading requires examining the errors they correct and those they introduce.

title: Microsoft 365 Backup retention period extended to ten years
summary: Microsoft has extended the recovery window for its Microsoft 365 Backup service from two to ten years, according to The Register . The change applies to OneDrive and SharePoint. The recovery window for Exchange is still limited to two years. For users who want a full restore, Microsoft 365 Backup creates restore points every ten minutes for the past two weeks. For periods further back, weekly restore points are available for up to three months, six months, or several years — up to a maximum of ten. The ten-year limit applies to new recovery points; it is not possible to go back additional years in time. The default recovery window remains one year. For longer periods, administrators must configure their backup policies. The list price for the service is $0.15 per GB per month. This article originally appeared on Computer Sweden.

title: datasette-charts 0.4a0
summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.4a0 The new datasette-charts plugin has its own plugin hook to allow other plugins to define new chart types, but I hadn't actually used it for anything yet. I had Claude Opus 5.5 build an experimental plugins just to try out the hook and it came up with a bunch of friction points in the design. This release addresses those, which should make building additional chart plugins a whole lot more ergonomic. I've also added a website for the plugin, at charts.datasette.io . The new website includes a tutorial for plugin authors , and a gallery showing all of the core charts and annotations, each one linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite . Tags: datasette-charts , datasette , visualization , datasette-lite
